children.note: How Kenyan law treats marriage, family property, divorce, children, and who inherits when someone dies. A draft study aid for law students, not legal advice.

nodeData.note: How Kenyan law treats marriage, family property, divorce, children, and who inherits when someone dies. A draft study aid for law students, not legal advice.

children.note: Start here: what the course covers and why it touches almost every Kenyan family.

children.topic: The law of home and family
children.note: Rules on who is married, who owns the family property, who looks after the children and who gets a person's property when they die.

manas.q: What does family law cover?

children.note: Succession (inheritance) decides who receives a dead person's property, and who manages it until it is shared out.

manas.q: What is the law of succession about?

children.note: Most people meet the law here: a wedding, a separation, a parent's death. Quarrels over a family shamba in Kiambu after the father dies are a very common kind of court case.
Kenya recognises customary, Islamic, Hindu, Christian and civil marriage together. All must fit within the Constitution. This mix is called legal pluralism.
Constitutional law (rights and equality), contract (agreements between spouses) and property ideas all come back in this course.
Where the rules come from: the Constitution 2010, a handful of Acts, and the courts.

The family is the basic unit of society. Adults may marry only with both people's free consent. Spouses have equal rights when they marry, during the marriage and when it ends. Parliament must recognise religious and customary marriage systems that fit the Constitution.

manas.q: What does Article 45 say about the rights of spouses?

children.note: Every child has rights to a name, education, basic needs, protection from abuse and parental care. Mother and father share responsibility whether married or not. The child's best interests come first.

manas.q: Which principle does Article 53 put first in matters about a child?

children.note: Everyone is equal before the law. Women and men must be treated equally, and the State may not discriminate on grounds including marital status.

Article 60 calls for an end to gender discrimination in land law and custom. Article 68 asks Parliament to protect matrimonial property, especially the matrimonial home, and the dependants of people who die holding land.
Kadhis' courts decide Muslim law questions of personal status, marriage, divorce and inheritance, but only where all parties are Muslim and agree to go there.

manas.q: When can a Kadhi's court hear a family dispute?

children.note: Five statutes do most of the work in this course.
Brings Kenya's marriage laws into one Act. Covers the kinds of marriage, who may marry, registration, separation and divorce.
Says what counts as matrimonial property and how it is shared when a marriage ends.
The main law on children: parental responsibility, custody, maintenance, adoption, guardianship and the Children's Court. The current Act dates from 2022.
Covers wills, sharing property when there is no will (intestacy), grants of representation and provision for dependants.
Lets a person facing abuse at home get a protection order from court.
Magistrates' courts and the High Court hear most family and succession cases. Children's matters go to Children's Courts. Muslims who agree may use the Kadhis' courts.
How a marriage is made, who may marry, and what makes a marriage void.
The Marriage Act 2014 recognises Christian, civil, customary, Hindu and Islamic marriage. All have the same legal status once valid.

manas.q: Which five kinds of marriage does the Marriage Act 2014 recognise?

children.note: Celebrated in church by a licensed minister. It is monogamous: one husband, one wife.
Celebrated before the Registrar of Marriages or an authorised officer. Also monogamous.
Made by the customs of the couple's communities, such as dowry talks between families. It may be polygamous and must be registered.
Made under Islamic law. A man may take more than one wife. Disputes may go to a Kadhi's court.
Made by Hindu rites. It is monogamous.
Christian, civil and Hindu marriages are monogamous. Customary and Islamic marriages may be polygamous. A wife's veto on a new wife was dropped from the final 2014 Act.

manas.q: Which kinds of marriage in Kenya may be polygamous?

children.note: Both people must be at least 18, must freely agree, must not be close relatives, and must not already be in a monogamous marriage.

manas.q: What is the minimum age for marriage in Kenya?

children.note: The Act requires every marriage to be registered, customary ones included. A marriage certificate is the easiest proof that you are married.
A void marriage was never valid, for example one with a 16-year-old or a close relative. A voidable marriage is valid until a court cancels it, for example where it was never consummated.

manas.q: What is the difference between a void and a voidable marriage?

children.note: Living together does not by itself make a marriage under the Act. Courts have sometimes presumed a marriage from long cohabitation, but apply this narrowly; check the latest Supreme Court decisions.
Who owns what in a marriage, and the ways a marriage ends.
The matrimonial home or homes, household goods, and other property the couple acquired together during the marriage.

manas.q: What counts as matrimonial property?

children.note: Each spouse's share follows what they contributed. Money counts, and so does unpaid work: childcare, running the home, working the family farm.

manas.q: Does unpaid work at home count as contribution to matrimonial property?

children.note: Article 45 gives spouses equal rights. Kenyan courts have read this as equal standing, not an automatic 50:50 split; the shares still depend on contribution. Check current appellate guidance.
The Matrimonial Property Act has rules for sharing property where a man has more than one wife, so that each wife's contribution is respected.
A marriage ends by death, by divorce, or by a court declaring it void. Judicial separation lets spouses live apart while still married.
A court order that ends a valid marriage.
A court order that a marriage was void, or cancels a voidable one.
A court order that spouses may live apart; the marriage continues.

For Christian, civil and Hindu marriages the grounds include adultery, cruelty, desertion, exceptional depravity and irretrievable breakdown. Customary and Islamic marriages are dissolved under their own rules, through court.

manas.q: Name three grounds for divorce in a Christian or civil marriage.

children.note: For customary marriages the Act expects the couple to try conciliation, often through elders, before a court ends the marriage.
A court can order one spouse to support the other, looking at each person's needs and means. Either husband or wife may be ordered to pay.

manas.q: Can a wife be ordered to maintain her husband in Kenya?

children.note: How the law protects children and shares parenting duties.
Anyone under 18 years of age.

manas.q: Who is a child in Kenyan law?

children.note: In every decision about a child, the court asks what is best for the child, not what the parents want. This comes from Article 53 and the Children Act.
The duties and powers of a parent: food, shelter, school, health care and guidance. Both parents share it, married or not.

manas.q: Do unmarried fathers have parental responsibility in Kenya?

children.note: Custody decides where the child lives; access lets the other parent spend time with the child. The court decides by the child's best interests.
Both parents must pay towards the child's needs according to their means. A court can order payment.
A court order that permanently moves all parental responsibility to the adopters. It needs proper consents and court approval; paying for a child is forbidden.
A guardian takes on a parent's role when a parent dies or cannot act. A parent may name one in a will, or the court may appoint one.
Children facing abuse, neglect or harmful practices such as child marriage or FGM can be protected by the Children's Court.
Courts listen to a child's own wishes, giving them more weight as the child grows older and understands more.
What happens to a person's property when they die: wills, no-will rules, grants and dependants.
Learn these first; every answer uses them.
Testate: the person died leaving a valid will. Intestate: they died without one, so the Act decides who inherits.

manas.q: What does it mean to die intestate?

children.note: An executor is named in the will to manage the estate. An administrator is appointed by the court when there is no will or no executor.

manas.q: What is the difference between an executor and an administrator?

children.note: A will lets a person choose who gets their property after death.
It must be in writing, signed by the maker (testator), and witnessed by at least two people. The maker must be an adult of sound mind acting freely.

manas.q: How many witnesses does a written will need in Kenya?

children.note: Kenya accepts a spoken will in narrow cases: made before two or more witnesses, and the maker dies within three months.
The maker must understand what a will does, what they own and who has a claim on them, free of delusions. See Banks v Goodfellow.
A will made through fraud, coercion, undue influence or mistake can be set aside by the court.
Add a codicil (a signed, witnessed change), make a new will, or deliberately destroy the old one.
The Law of Succession Act sets out who inherits when there is no valid will.
With a spouse and children, the spouse keeps personal and household effects plus a life interest in the rest. When the life interest ends, the children share it.

manas.q: Under intestacy, what does a surviving spouse with children receive?

children.note: The right to use and benefit from property for life, without owning it outright. Selling land needs the court's consent. The Act ends a widow's life interest on remarriage; critics say this clashes with Article 27.
The Act makes no difference between sons and daughters, married or unmarried. A custom that excludes daughters cannot override it.

manas.q: Can a married daughter inherit from her father under intestacy?

children.note: The estate goes to parents, then brothers and sisters, then other relatives, and finally to the State.
The estate is split between the 'houses': each wife and her children form a house, and each wife also counts as a unit.
The Act's distribution rules generally do not apply to a Muslim's estate; Islamic law does, often through a Kadhi's court.
A court order giving someone legal power to deal with the estate.
Given to the executor named in a valid will.
Given where there is no will, usually to the spouse or a close relative. Families often bring a letter from the local chief listing the survivors.
After a waiting period the court confirms the grant and approves how the estate will be shared. Only then can land be transferred to heirs.

manas.q: What must happen before an administrator can transfer estate land to heirs?

children.note: Dealing with a dead person's property without a grant, such as selling Mzee's cows or leasing his plot, is against the law.
People the deceased supported (spouse, children, sometimes parents or others) can ask the court for reasonable provision if the will or intestacy leaves them short.

manas.q: Who can apply for reasonable provision from an estate?

children.topic: Freedom to make a will is limited
children.note: You may leave property to whoever you like, but the court can rewrite the shares to protect dependants you left out.
Classic cases to know. English cases persuade Kenyan courts but do not bind them.

An English court refused to treat a polygamous Utah union as a marriage and defined marriage as a voluntary lifelong union of one man and one woman. Kenya differs: the Marriage Act 2014 recognises polygamous unions.

The House of Lords said judges dividing assets on divorce should test their result against a 'yardstick of equality', so a homemaker is not treated worse than an earner. Kenya instead uses contribution under the Matrimonial Property Act.

manas.q: What 'yardstick' did White v White introduce?

children.note: The House of Lords held that a child under 16 with enough understanding can consent to medical advice without a parent. It shows the child's growing say in their own life.
Set the classic test for the mental capacity to make a will: understand the act, the property and the people with claims, with no delusion warping the choice.

manas.q: Which case sets the test for capacity to make a will?

children.note: Kenya's Court of Appeal let Luo clan custom decide where a prominent lawyer was buried, over his widow's wishes, saying custom applies unless repugnant to justice and morality. Decided long before the 2010 Constitution.
Add the leading Kenyan decisions from Kenya Law (kenyalaw.org).
How to set out an answer, with a worked Kenyan example and common traps.
Issue (the legal question), Rule (Constitution, Act, case), Application (apply the rule to these facts), Conclusion (a clear answer).

manas.q: What do the letters IRAC stand for?

children.note: A short practice question on intestacy.
Mzee Kamau dies without a will. He leaves a widow, two sons and a married daughter. The sons say the daughter has no share because she married out.
Does the married daughter have a share in her father's estate?
The Law of Succession Act treats all children alike. Article 27 bans sex discrimination. The widow takes a life interest first.
Her marriage does not remove her status as his child. The custom the sons rely on cannot override the Act or the Constitution.
She shares equally with her brothers once the widow's life interest ends; the widow should seek a grant and then confirmation.
Equal rights in Article 45 do not mean each spouse automatically gets half. Show contribution.
Divorce grounds, polygamy and the court used all depend on the kind of marriage. Name it first.
If the deceased was Muslim, ask whether Islamic law and the Kadhi's court apply before using the intestacy rules.
Heirs often sell or subdivide too early. Without a confirmed grant this is intermeddling.

children.topic: Trap: parents' wishes over the child
children.note: The test is always the child's best interests, not what either parent prefers.

children.note: The rules on what a court may hear, who must prove what, and how strongly. In Kenya the main source is the Evidence Act, read with the fair-trial rights in the Constitution. A study aid, not legal advice.

nodeData.note: The rules on what a court may hear, who must prove what, and how strongly. In Kenya the main source is the Evidence Act, read with the fair-trial rights in the Constitution. A study aid, not legal advice.

children.note: Start here: what counts as evidence and why the rules exist.

children.topic: How facts are proved in court
children.note: Evidence is anything that helps a court decide whether a fact is true: what witnesses say, documents and objects.

manas.q: What is evidence?

children.topic: Facts in issue vs relevant facts
children.note: Facts in issue are what the case turns on (was the matatu driver speeding?). Relevant facts help prove them (long skid marks on the road).

manas.q: What is the difference between a fact in issue and a relevant fact?

children.note: Evidence comes in a few forms; most cases mix them.
What a witness says in court, usually on oath.
Writing or records offered to prove what they contain: a receipt, a title deed, a WhatsApp message.
A physical object the court can look at, such as a panga, a damaged side mirror or CCTV footage.
Direct evidence proves a fact straight away (I saw him take the phone). Circumstantial evidence points to it by inference (the phone was found in his bag).

manas.q: What is circumstantial evidence?

children.note: To keep trials fair, to keep out unreliable or unfairly prejudicial material, and to stop cases running forever.
The same Evidence Act applies to both, but criminal trials add strong constitutional protections for the accused.
Where Kenyan evidence law comes from.
Kenya's main evidence statute. It covers relevance, proof and presumptions, confessions, documents and electronic records, and witnesses.
An accused person is presumed innocent, need not testify, may refuse to give self-incriminating evidence, must get advance notice of the prosecution evidence and may challenge it.
Evidence gathered by breaking a Bill of Rights right must be left out if using it would make the trial unfair or harm justice. It is a test, not an automatic ban.

manas.q: When must evidence obtained in breach of rights be excluded in Kenya?

children.note: An arrested person must be told of the right to stay silent, and cannot be forced to confess or make an admission that could be used against them.

manas.q: What does Article 49 say about confessions by arrested persons?

children.note: The Criminal Procedure Code and the Sexual Offences Act add rules for criminal trials; the Civil Procedure Act and Rules govern civil cases.
Kenyan courts often cite English and Commonwealth cases on evidence. They persuade but do not bind; the Evidence Act and Constitution come first.
The first two questions for any piece of evidence.
Evidence is relevant if it makes a fact in issue more or less likely. Irrelevant evidence is never admitted.

manas.q: When is evidence relevant?

children.note: Admissible evidence is relevant and is not shut out by any rule, such as the hearsay rule or a privilege.

manas.q: Is every relevant fact admissible?

children.note: Words or acts so closely tied to an event that they form part of it, like a passenger shouting 'the brakes have failed!' as the matatu crashes.

manas.q: What is res gestae?

children.note: Once evidence is let in, the court decides how much to trust it. Admitted evidence can still carry little weight.
Older English common law usually let relevant evidence in however it was found. Kenya now applies the Article 50(4) fairness test instead.
Disputes about whether evidence can be used are decided by the judge, often in a 'trial within a trial'.
Who has to prove a fact, how strongly, and facts that need no proof.
The duty to persuade the court on an issue. In criminal cases it rests on the prosecution throughout. See Woolmington v DPP.

manas.q: Who carries the legal burden of proof in a criminal case?

children.note: The duty to produce enough evidence to make an issue worth considering, for example raising self-defence. It can move between parties.

manas.q: What is an evidential burden?

children.note: In a civil case the person making a claim, say the duka owner suing for unpaid goods, must usually prove it.
The criminal standard. The court must be sure of guilt; a real, sensible doubt means acquittal.

manas.q: What is the standard of proof in a criminal case?

children.note: The civil standard: is the claim more likely true than not? Lord Denning put it this way in Miller v Minister of Pensions.

manas.q: What is the standard of proof in a civil case?

children.note: Some laws make the accused prove a particular fact, such as one only they would know. Even then they need only reach the civil standard.
A rule that lets a court assume one fact from another until disproved, e.g. a person unheard of for seven years by those who would expect news may be presumed dead.
Can be knocked down by evidence, like the presumption of innocence.
Cannot be challenged, whatever the evidence; they are really fixed rules of law.
Facts so well known that no proof is needed, such as Nairobi being Kenya's capital or which day of the week a date fell on.

manas.q: What is judicial notice?

children.note: Facts a party admits need no proof. Estoppel stops a party from denying something they led another to believe and rely on.
The main exclusionary rules: hearsay, confessions, character and opinion.
Second-hand statements.
A statement made outside court, repeated in court to prove it is true. 'Wanjiru told me Otieno took the money' is hearsay if offered to prove he took it.

manas.q: What is hearsay?

children.note: The person who made the statement is not in court, so they cannot be cross-examined or watched by the court.

children.topic: Proving words were said is fine
children.note: If the point is only that the words were spoken, not that they were true, it is not hearsay. See Subramaniam v Public Prosecutor.
A dead person's statement about the cause of their death can be admitted. Unlike older English law, Kenyan law does not require that the speaker expected to die.
Business records, statements against the maker's own interest and public records can also come in, as the Evidence Act allows.
Admissions of guilt by the accused.
A statement by an accused that admits the offence or strongly suggests guilt.
A confession caused by threats, violence, promises or tricks by a person in authority is shut out.

manas.q: Why would a court reject a confession?

children.note: Kenya has strict rules on who may record a confession and how. Check the Evidence Act and its rules on out-of-court confessions.
If an accused later takes back a confession, courts look for other evidence supporting it before relying on it.
One accused's confession can count against another only with great caution, and never alone.
Evidence about what kind of person someone is.
That the accused has a past conviction does not prove they did it this time, and it can unfairly sway the court.
Past similar acts may come in if they are truly relevant, such as showing a pattern that rebuts a defence. See Makin v A-G for New South Wales.
An accused may show good character to support credibility and the unlikelihood of guilt; this may open the door to bad character in reply.
Who may say what they think, not just what they saw.
Ordinary witnesses say what they saw or heard; drawing conclusions is the court's job.

manas.q: What is the general rule on opinion evidence?

children.note: A qualified expert (doctor, handwriting examiner, ballistics officer) may give an opinion within their field. The court weighs it and is not bound by it.

manas.q: Is a court bound to accept an expert's opinion?

children.note: A non-expert may say someone looked drunk or that handwriting is a friend's they know well.
Who can testify, how they are questioned, privilege, and documents.
A competent witness can understand questions and give sensible answers. A court tests a young child's understanding first (voir dire).

manas.q: What makes a witness competent?

children.note: A compellable witness can be forced to testify. The accused cannot be forced to give evidence; a spouse may be compelled only in limited cases.

manas.q: Can an accused person be compelled to testify?

children.note: Three stages.
The party who called the witness asks open questions to draw out their story.
The other side tests the story and may ask leading questions.
The calling party clears up points raised in cross-examination; no new topics.
A question that suggests its answer ('You saw him at Gikomba, didn't you?'). Not allowed in chief, allowed in cross.

manas.q: When are leading questions allowed?

children.note: Some evidence needs support from another source before a court relies on it. Courts take special care with one witness identifying a stranger at night.
The right to refuse to reveal some information.
What a client tells their advocate for legal advice stays confidential. The privilege belongs to the client, and only the client can waive it. See Greenough v Gaskell.

manas.q: Who can waive legal professional privilege?

children.note: A person may refuse to answer questions that would expose them to a criminal charge.
What one spouse tells the other during marriage is generally protected from disclosure.
The State may withhold material whose release would harm national security or public interest; the court has the final say.
Rules for writing and records.
Primary evidence is the original document. Secondary evidence, like a photocopy, is used only when the original cannot be produced.

manas.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary documentary evidence?

children.note: Where terms are written down, such as a sale agreement, a party usually cannot use spoken evidence to change them.
M-Pesa records, emails and phone data are admissible. The Evidence Act usually requires a certificate describing how the record was produced.

manas.q: What usually accompanies electronic evidence in a Kenyan court?

children.note: Official records, like a land register extract, can be proved by certified copies.
Classic cases to know. English and Commonwealth cases persuade Kenyan courts but do not bind them.
The House of Lords held that the prosecution must prove guilt; an accused does not have to prove a killing was an accident. The 'golden thread' of criminal law.

manas.q: Which case calls the prosecution's duty to prove guilt a 'golden thread'?

children.note: Lord Denning described the civil standard as 'more probable than not'.

The Privy Council let in evidence of other babies' bodies at the accused's former homes. It set the rule that past similar acts are admissible only if relevant to an issue, not just to show bad character.
The Privy Council held that a statement offered only to prove it was said, not that it is true, is not hearsay.
An early English case grounding lawyer-client privilege in the needs of justice: people will not seek legal help if their words can be used against them.
Add the leading Kenyan decisions from Kenya Law (kenyalaw.org).
How to set out an answer, with a worked Kenyan example and common traps.
Issue (the evidence question), Rule (Evidence Act, Constitution, case), Application (to these facts), Conclusion (admitted or not, and why).

manas.q: What do the letters IRAC stand for?

children.note: A short practice question on confessions.
Kip is arrested over a stolen motorbike. At the station an officer slaps him and promises bail if he 'cooperates'. Kip signs a confession. There is little other evidence.
Can the prosecution rely on Kip's confession?
A confession must be voluntary. Article 49 bars forced confessions; Article 50(4) excludes evidence obtained in breach of rights if it makes the trial unfair.
The slap and the bail promise are violence and an inducement. Using the confession would make the trial unfair.
The court should exclude it after a trial within a trial; without other evidence Kip should be acquitted.
Relevance is only step one. Always ask whether an exclusionary rule applies.

children.topic: Trap: every repeated statement is hearsay
children.note: Ask why the words are offered. If not for their truth, they are not hearsay.
In a criminal case the legal burden stays on the prosecution. The accused at most carries an evidential burden, unless a statute says otherwise.

children.topic: Trap: using US or English rules
children.note: Cite the Evidence Act and Constitution first. Foreign rules, such as US 'fruit of the poisonous tree', are only comparisons.
Short videos and trusted pages to go deeper.
Lectures found on YouTube; Kenyan ones explain the Evidence Act.
A Kenyan tutor explains what evidence is and its types under the Evidence Act.
Explains facts in issue, relevant facts, relevance and admissibility.
A long Kenyan revision session covering the whole course.
A clear lecture on what hearsay is and why it is excluded.
A lecture on when character evidence can and cannot be used.
Pages that loaded on the day this map was made.
The full text of the fair-hearing Article of the Constitution.
Overview of relevance, exclusion, witnesses, hearsay and burdens.
The hearsay rule and its exceptions across common-law countries.
Legal and evidential burdens and the standards of proof.
Facts a court accepts without proof, with examples.

nodeData.note: Sale of goods, hire purchase and agency.

children.note: How the law governs selling goods, buying on hire purchase and acting for others (agency) in Kenya. A draft study aid for review, not legal advice.

nodeData.note: How the law governs selling goods, buying on hire purchase and acting for others (agency) in Kenya. A draft study aid for review, not legal advice.

children.note: The law of buying, selling and paying in business. It grows out of contract law from Year 1, with special rules for goods, credit and people who act for others.
Every sale, hire purchase deal or agency starts as a contract. Commercial law adds extra rules on top of the basic contract rules you learnt in Year 1.
From a duka selling sugar to a bank financing a matatu, trade depends on clear rules about who owns goods, who carries loss and who can sign for whom.
The Council of Legal Education lists this course as Commercial Law including sale of goods, hire purchase and agency. Those three are the heart of this map.

manas.q: Which three topics does the CLE core course on Commercial Law expressly include?

children.note: Kenya's commercial statutes were modelled on older English Acts, so English cases are often cited as persuasive. Kenyan Acts and courts have the final word in Kenya.
A sale of goods is a contract where the seller transfers ownership of goods to the buyer for money (the price). The Sale of Goods Act sets the default rules.
How a sale of goods contract comes into being and what counts as goods and price.
Ownership of goods passes for a money price. Swapping goods for goods (barter) or hiring them is not a sale.

manas.q: What two things make a contract a 'sale of goods'?

children.note: In a sale, ownership passes now. In an agreement to sell, it passes later or when a condition is met, for example when a farmer's maize is harvested.
Movable things you can touch: a phone, a cow, a bag of cement. Land and money are not goods.
Usually agreed by the parties. If no price is fixed, the buyer generally pays a reasonable price.
If specific goods have already perished when the contract is made, without the seller knowing, the contract is usually void. Perishing later may end an agreement to sell.
Promises the law reads into every sale even if no one said them out loud.
A condition is a major term: breach lets the buyer reject the goods. A warranty is a minor term: breach gives only damages.

manas.q: What is the difference between a condition and a warranty in a sale of goods?

children.note: The seller promises they have the right to sell. Selling a stolen motorbike breaks this term.

manas.q: What does the implied term as to title promise?

children.note: Goods sold by description must match it. 'Pishori rice' must be pishori. Reliance on the description matters.

manas.q: Under the implied term on description, what must goods do?

children.note: A business seller's goods must be of decent quality. Kenya's older-style Act speaks of merchantable quality; England now uses 'satisfactory quality'. Only business sellers are bound.

manas.q: Which implied term uses the phrase 'merchantable quality' in older-style Acts like Kenya's?

children.note: If the buyer tells a business seller what the goods are for and relies on their skill, the goods must be fit for that purpose.
When you buy from a sample, the bulk must match the sample and you must have a fair chance to compare them.
Sellers sometimes try to exclude these terms in small print. Courts read such clauses strictly, and consumer law limits them, especially against consumers.
Property means ownership. Risk means who bears the loss if goods are damaged. The timing of both matters a lot.
The parties decide when ownership passes. If they say nothing, the Act gives default rules.

manas.q: What is the main rule on when property in goods passes?

children.note: Specific goods are identified at the contract, like 'this red car'. Unascertained goods, like '50 bags of sugar from the store', cannot pass until they are identified.

manas.q: Why can property in unascertained goods not pass at once?

children.note: By default, whoever owns the goods carries the risk of loss, even if the other party holds them. Parties can agree otherwise.

manas.q: By default, who bears the risk of loss of goods?

children.note: A seller can agree to keep ownership until full payment. This is a retention of title (Romalpa) clause, useful when a buyer goes insolvent.
General rule: a seller who does not own goods cannot pass ownership, even to an honest buyer. The real owner keeps title.
If a thief sells your phone at a market, the buyer does not become owner. You can claim it back.

manas.q: What does the nemo dat rule say?

children.note: If the owner's words or conduct led the buyer to believe the seller could sell, the owner may be stopped (estopped) from denying it.
A rogue who gets goods by fraud has voidable title. If they sell to an honest buyer before the owner cancels the deal, the buyer gets good title.

manas.q: When can a buyer from a fraudster with voidable title keep the goods?

children.note: A dealer trusted with the owner's goods may pass good title to an honest buyer in the ordinary course of business.

children.topic: Exception: seller or buyer in possession
children.note: A seller who keeps goods after selling, or a buyer who gets them before owning them, may sometimes pass title to an honest third person.
England abolished the old open-market exception in 1995. Students should check the Kenyan Act's text before relying on it in Kenya.
What each side must do, and what happens when one fails.
The seller must deliver the goods; the buyer must accept them and pay. Unless agreed otherwise, the two happen together.
A buyer who says they accept, acts like the owner, or keeps goods too long without complaint loses the right to reject, but can still claim damages.

manas.q: How can a buyer lose the right to reject goods?

children.note: Sue for the price, claim damages if the buyer refuses to accept, and as an unpaid seller hold onto goods (lien), stop them in transit or resell in some cases.

manas.q: Name two remedies of an unpaid seller.

children.note: Reject the goods for breach of condition, claim damages for non-delivery or poor goods, and rarely ask the court to order delivery (specific performance).
Buying on instalments where you hire the goods first and become owner only when you finish paying. Common for cars, matatus and farm machines in Kenya.
You pay a deposit, use the goods and pay instalments. Ownership passes at the end, often by a small option-to-buy payment.

manas.q: When does a hirer under hire purchase become the owner?

children.note: Often a dealer sells the car to a finance company, which then lets it on hire purchase to you. Your contract is with the finance company.

children.topic: Not the same as a sale
children.note: Under hire purchase you are a hirer, not an owner, until the end. So you generally cannot sell the goods and pass good title meanwhile.

manas.q: Why can a hirer usually not pass good title before paying in full?

children.note: Pay off early, usually with a rebate; return the goods subject to limits; and sue if the owner wrongly repossesses.
If the hirer defaults, the owner may keep instalments paid, claim money due and repossess. The law can require a court order first.
Kenya has a Hire Purchase Act that sets formal rules for these agreements and protects hirers, for example on repossession. Read the Act itself for the exact thresholds.
One person (the agent) acts for another (the principal) to make deals with third parties. Think of a shop manager ordering stock for the owner.
Principal: the boss. Agent: the one acting. Third party: the outsider who deals with the agent. Three relationships arise.
By agreement, by later approval (ratification), by necessity in emergencies, or by the principal's conduct (estoppel).
The usual way: the principal appoints the agent, in writing or by word of mouth.
An agent acts without authority, and the principal later approves the act. The approval works backwards as if authority existed.

manas.q: What is ratification in agency?

children.note: In an emergency, a person holding another's goods may act to save them when they cannot reach the owner.
Authority decides whether the principal is bound.
Authority truly given, either in words (express) or understood from the job (implied).

manas.q: What two forms can actual authority take?

children.note: The principal makes it look as if the agent has authority, the third party relies on it, and the principal is bound.

manas.q: What three things must be shown for apparent (ostensible) authority?

children.note: A principal may be bound by acts usually within an agent's type of job, even if privately forbidden. The leading case is much criticised.
Obey instructions, use care and skill, act personally, avoid conflicts of interest, take no secret profit and account for money.

manas.q: Name three duties an agent owes the principal.

children.note: Pay the agreed commission and reimburse proper expenses.

children.topic: Who is liable to the third party
children.note: Usually the principal, if the agent acted within authority. An agent who claims authority they lack can be personally liable.
By agreement, finishing the task, or by law, such as death, insanity or bankruptcy of a party.
Where Kenyan commercial law comes from: the Constitution, Acts of Parliament and the courts.

Consumers have rights to goods and services of reasonable quality, to information, to protection of health, safety and money, and to compensation for loss or injury. Parliament must make consumer laws.

manas.q: Which Article of the Constitution of Kenya 2010 protects consumer rights?

children.note: Protects the right to own property and bars arbitrary taking. It is a reminder that ownership of goods is a protected right.
Kenya's main statute on sale of goods. It follows the older English model, so English cases on similar words are often persuasive.
Governs hire purchase agreements in Kenya, including their form and the hirer's protections.
Protects consumers against unfair and misleading business practices. It builds on Article 46 and sits alongside the Sale of Goods Act.
Cheques and bills of exchange can pass from hand to hand. An honest holder who pays value can take free of earlier defects, an exception to nemo dat.
Add the leading Kenyan decisions from Kenya Law (kenyalaw.org).
Classic common-law cases taught in Kenyan commercial law courses. They are persuasive, not binding, in Kenya.
A man got dermatitis from new woollen underwear. The Privy Council held the shop liable on fitness for purpose because he relied on its skill, and the maker liable in negligence.

manas.q: What did Grant v Australian Knitting Mills decide about the retailer?

children.note: A rogue posed as a known firm by letter. The contract was void for mistaken identity, so the honest later buyer got no title and returned the goods.

manas.q: Why did the innocent buyer lose in Cundy v Lindsay?

children.note: A car owner paid by a bad cheque told the police and AA at once. This clear act cancelled the voidable deal before the car reached a later buyer.

manas.q: How did Mr Caldwell rescind the contract with a vanished fraudster?

children.note: A supplier kept ownership of foil until paid. When the buyer became insolvent, the supplier recovered its unused foil and sale proceeds ahead of other creditors.

manas.q: What did the Romalpa case decide about retention of title clauses?

children.note: A pub owner was liable for cigars ordered by his manager, though privately forbidden, because such orders were usual for a manager. Heavily criticised today.

manas.q: Why was the owner liable in Watteau v Fenwick?

children.note: Apparent authority works like estoppel: a representation, reliance on it, and a change of position by the third party.
A painting was wrongly described, but the expert buyer had not relied on the description, so the description term was not breached.
Use IRAC: Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion. Take each party and each issue in turn.
Wanjiru lends her motorbike to Otieno to repair. Otieno sells it to Kamau at a Kiambu market. Kamau paid fair value and suspected nothing. Can Wanjiru recover it?
Did Kamau get good title from someone who did not own the motorbike?
Nemo dat: no one passes better title than they have, subject to exceptions such as estoppel and the mercantile agent rule.
Otieno owned nothing. Was he a dealer acting in the ordinary course of business? Did Wanjiru's conduct mislead Kamau? Probably not on these facts.
Wanjiru can likely recover the motorbike; Kamau's claim is against Otieno. Always say what more facts could change the answer.
Points that lose marks easily.
Holding goods is not owning them. Ask who owns, not who holds.
Quality and fitness terms bind only sellers acting in the course of business, not your neighbour selling an old sofa.
A void contract (Cundy) passes no title; a voidable one (fraud face to face) can pass title until cancelled. Say which applies.

children.topic: Treating hire purchase as a sale
children.note: A hirer is not yet owner. This changes nemo dat and repossession answers.
Cite the Kenyan Act and Article 46 before English cases. English cases persuade; they do not bind Kenyan courts.

Lectures found on YouTube; check each against the Kenyan Acts.

nodeData.topic: Law of Business Associations and Insolvency
nodeData.note: How people run businesses together in Kenya, from partnerships to companies under the Companies Act 2015, and what happens when they fail under the Insolvency Act 2015. A draft study aid, not legal advice.

children.note: The legal forms people use to run a business together, and what happens when a business cannot pay its debts.
Sole trader, partnership, limited liability partnership or company. The choice affects who owns, who decides and who pays if it fails.
A mama mboga, a law firm and Safaricom all need a legal form. Picking the right one protects owners and creditors.

manas.q: Name four legal forms a business in Kenya can take.

children.note: Article 36 protects the right to form and join associations, and requires fair process before a registration is cancelled.

manas.q: Which Article of the Constitution protects freedom of association?

children.note: The Partnership Act, Limited Liability Partnerships Act, Companies Act 2015 and Insolvency Act 2015 are the core statutes.

manas.q: Which two 2015 Acts govern Kenyan companies and insolvency?

children.topic: Insolvency is part of the course
children.note: The CLE lists this course as Law of Business Associations, to include Insolvency.
The simplest forms: one person in business, or several in business together.
One person owns and runs the business. No separate legal person exists, so all debts are the owner's personal debts.

manas.q: Is a sole trader's business a separate legal person?

children.note: Two or more people running a business in common to make a profit. It can arise from a written deed, a spoken deal or conduct alone.

manas.q: What are the elements of a partnership?

children.note: Each partner can usually bind the firm in ordinary business dealings, so choose partners carefully.
Partners are personally liable for the firm's debts, so a creditor can reach a partner's own house or car.

manas.q: What is the main risk of an ordinary partnership?

children.note: Unless agreed otherwise, partners share profits equally, all take part in management and are indemnified for proper business costs.
By agreement, expiry, a partner's death, or a court order. Assets go first to pay debts.
Kenya has its own Partnership Act, which follows the English model while also allowing limited partners.
A hybrid under Kenya's Limited Liability Partnerships Act: partners run it like a partnership, but the LLP is a legal person and partners' liability is limited.

manas.q: How does an LLP differ from an ordinary partnership?

children.note: A company is created by registration and becomes a legal person separate from its owners.
Founders file documents with the Registrar of Companies. The certificate of incorporation is the company's birth certificate.
Private or public; limited by shares, limited by guarantee or unlimited. Only public companies can offer shares to the public.
Under the Companies Act 2015, a private company may have a single member, like a one-person matatu business.
The company owns its property, makes contracts, sues and is sued in its own name.
A bootmaker turned his business into a company and held almost all shares. When it failed, the House of Lords held he was not liable for its debts: the company was a separate person.

manas.q: What principle did Salomon v Salomon establish?

children.note: A man owned nearly all shares and was the company's pilot. He could still be its employee, so his widow got compensation.

manas.q: Why could Mr Lee be an employee of his own company?

children.note: A sole shareholder insured timber in his own name, not the company's. His claim failed because the timber belonged to the company.
Shareholders lose only what they put in or promised for their shares. The company's creditors cannot chase their personal assets.

manas.q: What does 'limited liability' mean for a shareholder?

children.note: Rarely, courts look past the company to the people behind it.
The modern English test: the veil may be pierced only where a company is used to dodge a legal duty its controller already had.

manas.q: What is the modern English test for piercing the veil?

children.note: A former employee set up a company to break his promise not to compete. The court stopped him by injunction.
Courts cannot ignore Salomon just because justice seems to demand it; group companies are separate.
The UK Supreme Court narrowed true piercing to evasion of existing obligations. The family homes reached the wife through trust law instead.
Laws on fraudulent or wrongful trading can make directors personally liable when a company fails.
The company's rulebook and how money comes in and out.
The company's internal rules on meetings, directors and shares. Model articles apply where the company has not written its own.

manas.q: What are a company's articles of association?

children.note: The articles bind the company and its members like a contract, so members can enforce some of their rights.
A share is a unit of ownership, giving rights to dividends, votes and a slice of surplus on winding up.
Preference shares usually get dividends first but carry fewer votes. Ordinary shares carry the main risk and control.

manas.q: How do preference shares differ from ordinary shares?

children.note: A company should not hand its capital back to members except as the law allows. Dividends come from profits only.

manas.q: From what may a company pay dividends?

children.note: Companies borrow using debentures and give security. A fixed charge is over a specific asset; a floating charge hovers over changing assets like stock.

manas.q: What is the difference between a fixed and a floating charge?

children.note: Charges must be registered so that later lenders can see what is already pledged. Missing this can make the charge fail against a liquidator.
Who runs the company, who owns it, and how they make decisions.
People who manage the company day to day. A company secretary handles filings and records.
The Companies Act 2015 sets out directors' general duties, drawn from older case law.
Follow the constitution and use powers only for their proper purposes.
Act in good faith for the members as a whole, thinking of employees, suppliers, community and environment.

manas.q: Whose interests must a director promote under the codified duties?

children.note: Act as a reasonably careful director would, judged by the job and by the director's own knowledge.
No using company opportunities for yourself, no bribes from third parties, and declare interests in company deals.
Directors bought shares in a subsidiary and made profits through their office. They had to repay the profit even without fraud or loss to the company.

manas.q: Why did the directors in Regal (Hastings) have to repay their profit?

children.note: Members own the company, but the majority usually rules.
If directors wrong the company, the company itself is the proper claimant, not individual members. The majority may ratify.

manas.q: What is the proper plaintiff rule in Foss v Harbottle?

children.note: Illegal acts, bypassing a special majority, invading a member's personal rights, and fraud on the minority.
Kenya's Companies Act 2015 lets a member, with court permission, sue on the company's behalf for wrongs by directors.
A member whose interests are unfairly harmed by how the company is run can ask the court for a remedy, such as a buy-out.
Members decide key issues by resolution at meetings or in writing.
Passed by a simple majority of votes, for example to appoint a director.

manas.q: What majority does an ordinary resolution need?

children.note: Needs at least 75% of votes, for big decisions like changing the articles or a voluntary winding up.

manas.q: What majority does a special resolution need?

children.note: A regular meeting where members receive accounts and question directors. Rules differ for private and public companies.
What happens when a person or company cannot pay debts. Kenya's Insolvency Act 2015 covers both individuals and companies.
Unable to pay debts as they fall due (cash-flow test) or debts larger than assets (balance-sheet test).

manas.q: What are the two common tests for insolvency?

children.note: A court process for people who cannot pay. A trustee collects and shares out assets, and the person is later discharged.
A debtor and creditors agree a plan to pay part of the debts over time, avoiding bankruptcy or liquidation.
An administrator takes over to rescue the company or get creditors a better result. A moratorium stops creditors suing meanwhile.

manas.q: What is the main aim of administration?

children.note: The end of the road: a liquidator sells assets, pays creditors and the company is dissolved.
Started by members' special resolution. If solvent, members control it; if insolvent, creditors do.
Ordered by the court, usually on a creditor's petition for an unpaid debt.
Roughly: secured creditors, costs, preferential debts like wages, floating charge holders, unsecured creditors, then members last. Kenya's Act sets its own list.

manas.q: Who is paid last in a liquidation?

children.note: Directors who keep trading when they knew or should have known the company could not avoid insolvent liquidation can be made to contribute.

manas.q: When can directors be liable for wrongful trading?

children.note: A public officer who acts in many bankruptcies and liquidations, especially early on or where no private insolvency practitioner is appointed.
Cases above are English or Commonwealth decisions, persuasive in Kenya. Kenyan statutes and courts come first.
Kenya's company and insolvency Acts borrow heavily from English law, so Kenyan courts often cite English cases as persuasive, not binding.
Add the leading Kenyan decisions from Kenya Law (kenyalaw.org).
Kenyan law has its own Acts, registrar and procedures. Always cite the Companies Act 2015 or Insolvency Act 2015 before English authority.
Use IRAC: Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion.
Achieng owns 99% of Kiambu Feeds Ltd. The company owes a supplier KES 2m and is closing. Can the supplier sue Achieng personally?
Issue: is Achieng liable for the company's debt? Rule: separate personality (Salomon) and limited liability; the veil is lifted only in narrow cases.
Unless Achieng used the company to evade an existing duty, or trading rules apply, the supplier can claim only against the company, likely in liquidation.
Owning almost all shares does not make you the company. Keep person and company apart.

children.topic: Trap: lifting the veil too easily
children.note: Courts rarely pierce the veil. Unfairness alone is not enough.

manas.q: Is unfairness alone enough to lift the corporate veil?

children.note: Once a company nears insolvency, think of creditors and wrongful trading, not just shareholders.

nodeData.note: Fair administrative action, judicial review, natural justice and remedies.

children.note: The rules that keep government officers and public bodies within their powers and make them treat people fairly. In Kenya it rests on the Constitution 2010, the Fair Administrative Action Act 2015 and the High Court's power of judicial review.

nodeData.note: The rules that keep government officers and public bodies within their powers and make them treat people fairly. In Kenya it rests on the Constitution 2010, the Fair Administrative Action Act 2015 and the High Court's power of judicial review.

children.note: The starting point: who the "administration" is, and why its power needs limits.
It covers the everyday decisions of ministries, county offices, boards and agencies: licences, permits, dismissals, refunds.

manas.q: What does administrative law govern?

children.note: Like constitutional law it deals with the state and the citizen, not two private people. Constitutional law sets up power; administrative law polices how it is used day to day.
A county officer refuses to renew your matatu operating licence without telling you why. Administrative law asks: did the officer have the power, use it sensibly, and treat you fairly?
A public body can only do what the Constitution or an Act allows it to do. Acting outside that permission is acting beyond its powers (ultra vires).

manas.q: What does "ultra vires" mean?

children.topic: Why it matters: rule of law
children.note: Nobody in government is above the law. Courts can check officials so that power is used for the public, not for favouritism or spite.
In judicial review the court checks HOW the decision was made, not whether it was the best choice. On appeal a court may substitute its own answer.

manas.q: How is judicial review different from an appeal?

children.note: Where Kenyan administrative law comes from: the Constitution 2010, Acts of Parliament, and the courts.
Everyone has a right to administrative action that is quick, efficient, lawful, reasonable and fair in procedure. Kenya made good administration a constitutional right, which English law never did.

manas.q: What five qualities must administrative action have under Article 47?

children.note: If a decision has hurt, or may hurt, one of your rights, you can ask for the reasons in writing.

manas.q: When can a person demand written reasons under Article 47?

children.note: The Article told Parliament to pass a law giving effect to these rights, with review by a court or an independent tribunal, and promoting efficient administration.
The Act Parliament passed to give effect to Article 47. It sets out the duty to act fairly, the right to reasons, how to apply for review, and what the court can order.

manas.q: Which Act gives effect to Article 47?

children.note: Anyone with a dispute that the law can settle may have it decided at a fair, public hearing before a court or, where suitable, an independent tribunal.
Citizens can get information held by the state, and information held by others when needed to protect a right. Useful when you need the file behind a decision.
The High Court supervises lower courts and any body doing judicial or quasi-judicial work. It can call for their records and make orders to keep justice fair.

manas.q: Which Article gives the High Court supervisory jurisdiction?

children.note: Commission on Administrative Justice Act 2011 (the Ombudsman), Access to Information Act, and the Statutory Instruments Act (rules on delegated legislation). Ask your lecturer for the current versions.
In England judicial review is mostly judge-made common law. In Kenya it is also a constitutional right and a statutory procedure, so always start with Article 47 and the 2015 Act.
The reasons a court will use to strike down a decision. The classic list comes from the GCHQ case (1984); Kenya adds the statutory grounds in the 2015 Act.
Illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety, as listed by Lord Diplock in the GCHQ case. Proportionality was flagged as a possible fourth.

manas.q: What are Lord Diplock's three grounds of judicial review?

children.note: The decision-maker got the law wrong: no power at all, used a power for the wrong purpose, or misread the Act.

manas.q: What is the ground of illegality?

children.note: Example: a county clerk fines a shopkeeper when no law lets the clerk impose fines. The fine is void.
A power given for one aim cannot be used for another, such as using a land-planning power to punish a political rival.
Taking into account things that do not matter, or ignoring things that do, makes the decision unlawful.
Applying a rigid policy and refusing to listen to the particular case. The officer must keep an open mind.
A decision so unreasonable that no sensible authority could have made it. The bar is high: disagreeing with the decision is not enough.

manas.q: What is the Wednesbury test of unreasonableness?

children.note: The right steps were not followed: no hearing, bias, or a procedure required by the Act was skipped.

manas.q: What is procedural impropriety?

children.topic: Breaking the rules of natural justice
children.note: Not hearing the person, or a biased decision-maker. See the natural justice branch.
If an Act says "consult the public first" and the body skips it, the decision can be quashed.
Was the step taken no heavier than needed to reach a legitimate aim? Stronger than Wednesbury, and common where rights are limited.

manas.q: What does proportionality ask?

children.note: If a public body clearly promised something, or always followed a practice, it may not suddenly go back on it unfairly.

manas.q: What is a legitimate expectation?

children.note: An expectation to be consulted or heard before a change is made.
An expectation of the promised benefit itself, as in Coughlan's "home for life".
Two old common-law rules of fair procedure. In Kenya they also sit inside Article 47's promise of procedurally fair action.
No one should judge their own cause (nemo iudex in causa sua). The decision-maker must be impartial and be seen to be so.

manas.q: What is the rule against bias called in Latin?

children.note: A judge holding shares in a party was disqualified without asking whether he was really biased (Dimes v Grand Junction Canal, 1852).
Would a fair-minded, informed observer see a real possibility of bias? (Porter v Magill, 2001).

manas.q: What is the test for apparent bias in Porter v Magill?

children.topic: Justice must be seen to be done
children.note: Public confidence matters as much as actual fairness (R v Sussex Justices, ex p McCarthy, 1924).
Hear the other side (audi alteram partem). Before a decision hurts you, you should know the case and get a chance to answer.

manas.q: What does "audi alteram partem" require?

children.note: You must be told the gist of what is alleged against you, in time to prepare.
Usually in writing; an oral hearing is not always needed (Lloyd v McMahon, 1987).

children.topic: Example: school board expels a pupil
children.note: A board in Kiambu expels a pupil without letting the parents respond. That is a classic breach of the right to be heard.
English common law has no general duty to give reasons. Kenya's Article 47 gives a right to written reasons when rights are affected: a plain difference.
What a successful applicant actually gets. Remedies in judicial review are discretionary: the court may refuse them.
An order cancelling an unlawful decision so it has no effect. England renamed it a "quashing order" in 2004; Kenyan courts still use the old name.

manas.q: What does an order of certiorari do?

children.note: An order forcing a public body to do a public duty it is refusing to do, such as issuing a document it must issue.

manas.q: What does an order of mandamus do?

children.note: An order stopping a body from making an unlawful decision it is about to make.

manas.q: What does an order of prohibition do?

children.note: The court states what the legal position is, for example that a regulation is invalid, without ordering anything.
An injunction orders someone to do or stop something. Damages are possible in some cases, but are not the usual judicial review remedy.
Delay, a better alternative remedy (such as an appeal), or bad conduct by the applicant can lead the court to refuse relief.
Other ways of controlling the administration: tribunals, the Ombudsman, and checks on delegated legislation.
Specialist bodies that decide disputes in one area, such as rent or tax, more cheaply and quickly than courts. They must still act fairly and lawfully.

manas.q: Why does the state use tribunals?

children.note: The High Court can supervise tribunals because they do quasi-judicial work.
Kenya's Ombudsman, set up under the Commission on Administrative Justice Act 2011. It takes complaints about maladministration, such as delay, rudeness or unfair treatment by public offices.

manas.q: What is Kenya's Ombudsman officially called?

children.note: The Ombudsman is free, informal and can look at bad service that is not strictly illegal. It mostly recommends; a court can make binding orders.
Rules made by a minister or body under power given by an Act: regulations, rules, orders and county by-laws.

manas.q: What is delegated legislation?

children.note: Parliament sets the broad policy; the ministry fills in technical detail that changes often, like fees or forms.
Parliament can scrutinise and annul it, and courts can strike it down if it goes beyond the parent Act or breaks the Constitution.
Classic English cases that Kenyan courts and textbooks still use, plus Kenyan decisions for your reviewer to add.
A council let a cinema open on Sundays but banned under-15s. The court upheld the condition and set the test: only a decision no reasonable authority could make is irrational.
The government banned unions at an intelligence centre. The Lords held prerogative powers can be reviewed, but national security won; Lord Diplock set out the three grounds.

manas.q: What did the GCHQ case decide about prerogative powers?

children.note: A chief constable was sacked without a chance to defend himself. The Lords held natural justice applies to administrative decisions too.

manas.q: What did Ridge v Baldwin decide?

children.note: An Act said a tribunal's decisions could not be questioned. The Lords still reviewed it: a decision based on an error of law is no real decision, so the ouster clause did not protect it.

manas.q: What did Anisminic decide about ouster clauses?

children.note: A disabled woman was promised a "home for life", then the home was to close. Breaking the promise was an abuse of power: a substantive legitimate expectation.
Add the leading Kenyan decisions from Kenya Law (kenyalaw.org).
Use IRAC: Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion. Work through each ground in turn.
Nairobi county revokes Wanjiku's kiosk licence overnight after a rival, who is the officer's cousin, complains. She gets no notice and no reasons.
Was the revocation lawful, fair and reasonable, and what can Wanjiku ask the court for?
Article 47 and the Fair Administrative Action Act 2015; the grounds of review; the bias and hearing rules.
The officer's cousin gains, so a fair observer would see a real possibility of bias. No notice and no chance to reply breaks the right to be heard.
No written reasons despite her livelihood being hit. She could seek certiorari to quash the revocation and possibly mandamus to have her application reconsidered fairly.
The revocation is likely unlawful. Say "likely": courts have discretion, and check facts like delay or other remedies.
Common mistakes that lose marks.
Saying "the decision was wrong" is not a ground. Show illegality, irrationality, unfairness or another recognised ground.
In Kenya, start with Article 47 and the 2015 Act, then use English cases as support.
Certiorari cancels; mandamus compels; prohibition prevents. Match the remedy to what the client needs.
If an Act gives an appeal route, the court may expect you to use it first. Mention it.
Short videos on the grounds of review, then pages to read. UK videos explain the common law; check Kenyan differences.
The Law Academy gives a short overview of the main grounds of review.
The Law Academy explains the illegality ground with examples.
A longer English Law lecture on Wednesbury unreasonableness.
The Law Academy on unfair procedure and natural justice.
African Justice Systems lecture on the right to fair administrative action.
Wikipedia overview of grounds, standing and remedies.
The official text of the fair administrative action Article.
Wikipedia article on the bias and hearing rules, with many cases.
Wikipedia page on Kenya's Ombudsman.

nodeData.note: What law is: natural law, positivism, realism, justice and African jurisprudence.

children.note: The study of what law is, where its authority comes from, and how it should relate to morality and justice. It is the "big questions" course of the LLB, and gives you the vocabulary to argue about any rule you meet.

nodeData.note: The study of what law is, where its authority comes from, and how it should relate to morality and justice. It is the "big questions" course of the LLB, and gives you the vocabulary to argue about any rule you meet.

children.note: Legal theory: thinking about law itself rather than one area of rules.

children.topic: The central question: what is law?
children.note: Is a rule law because a ruler commands it, because society accepts it, or because it is just? Each school gives a different answer.

manas.q: What is the central question of jurisprudence?

children.note: Describes what law is and how legal systems work, like a map of the system.
Asks what law ought to be: when is a law just, and when should we obey it?

children.topic: Why a Kenyan student needs it
children.note: Courts interpreting the Constitution 2010 constantly face theory questions: values versus text, custom versus statute, rights versus majority will.
A rule says "no matatu in the CBD". Is it law because the county made it, because people obey it, or only if it is fair? That is jurisprudence in one line.
The oldest school: true law is connected to reason and morality, so an unjust rule is defective as law.
There are moral standards we can discover by reason, and human law should conform to them.

manas.q: What is the core claim of natural law theory?

children.note: Aristotle tied the good to human nature; Cicero described natural law as right reason agreeing with nature.
Thomas Aquinas linked eternal law (God's plan), natural law (our reasoned share of it), divine law (revealed) and human law (made by rulers).

manas.q: Name the kinds of law in Aquinas's scheme.

children.topic: Aquinas: unjust law is no law
children.note: An unjust law keeps only the outward look of law; it is a corruption of law (lex iniusta non est lex).

manas.q: What does "lex iniusta non est lex" mean?

children.note: John Finnis lists seven self-evident goods: life, knowledge, play, aesthetic experience, sociability, practical reasonableness and religion. Law exists to help people pursue them.

children.topic: Fuller: the inner morality of law
children.note: Lon Fuller argued that a system only counts as law if it meets certain procedural standards. This is a "procedural" natural law.
Rules should be general, published, not retroactive, clear, not contradictory, fairly stable, possible to obey, and applied as written.

manas.q: List Fuller's eight principles of legality.

children.note: Law is a social fact: what counts as law depends on how it was made, not on whether it is good.
Law and morality are separate questions. A rule can be valid law and still be unjust.

manas.q: What is the separation thesis?

children.note: Jeremy Bentham, an early positivist, wanted law studied as it is, then reformed by asking what produces the most happiness.
Law is a command from a sovereign whom people habitually obey, backed by a sanction (threat of punishment).

manas.q: How did John Austin define law?

children.note: His theory fits criminal law, but struggles with constitutions, international law and power-giving rules like contracts and wills.
In The Concept of Law (1961), H.L.A. Hart said law joins primary rules (how to behave) with secondary rules (how rules are recognised, changed and applied).

manas.q: What are primary and secondary rules in Hart's theory?

children.note: The master secondary rule that officials use to identify which rules are valid law.

manas.q: What is Hart's rule of recognition?

children.note: Hans Kelsen said each norm gets its validity from a higher norm, ending in an assumed basic norm (Grundnorm).

manas.q: What is Kelsen's Grundnorm?

children.note: Exclusive positivists (Raz) say law is identified by social sources only; inclusive positivists say a system may adopt moral tests.
Famous exchanges that sharpen the natural law versus positivism argument.
Two essays in the Harvard Law Review: Hart defended keeping law and morals apart; Fuller replied that law has a built-in morality.
In 1944 a wife reported her husband's anti-Hitler remarks to be rid of him. After the war a court convicted her, treating the Nazi law she relied on as offending basic justice.

children.topic: Hart vs Fuller on the informer
children.note: Hart said be honest: either punish her using a retroactive law, or let her go, and admit the moral cost. Fuller said the Nazi rules were not true law at all.
Ronald Dworkin argued law is not just rules: judges also apply principles, and the right answer comes from the best moral reading of the law.
A grandson poisoned his grandfather to inherit. The New York court refused him the estate: no one may profit from their own wrong, though no statute said so.

manas.q: What did Riggs v Palmer decide and why did Dworkin use it?

children.note: Dworkin's imaginary perfect judge finds the reading that best fits and justifies the whole law: "law as integrity" (Law's Empire, 1986).
Schools that look at what law does in real life, where it comes from, and whom it serves.
Law is what courts actually do. Study judges, not just rule books.
Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. saw law as predictions of what courts will in fact decide.

manas.q: How did Holmes describe law?

children.note: American realists who looked behind decisions to the judges themselves and their psychology.
A separate European tradition (Hägerström, Ross, Olivecrona) explaining law by empirical social facts.
Law grows out of a people's history and customs, not from a ruler's will.

children.topic: Savigny: the spirit of the people
children.note: Friedrich Carl von Savigny said each nation's law reflects its Volksgeist and opposed rushing into a German code.

manas.q: What did Savigny mean by Volksgeist?

children.note: Henry Maine's Ancient Law (1861) traced a move from roles fixed by birth and family to relations people choose by agreement.
Study law in light of the society around it.
Roscoe Pound saw law as a tool to balance competing individual and social interests and solve social problems.

manas.q: What did Roscoe Pound mean by social engineering?

children.note: Eugen Ehrlich and the European "free law" thinkers stressed the rules people actually live by.
Law reflects the economy and serves the class that owns the means of production.
The economic base shapes a legal and political superstructure built on top of it.

manas.q: In Marxist theory, is law part of the base or the superstructure?

children.note: Evgeny Pashukanis tied law to commodity exchange and said that under full communism law and state would wither away.
A 1970s US movement: legal decisions are political choices, rules rarely settle cases, and law tends to protect the powerful.

manas.q: What are the main claims of critical legal studies?

children.note: Asks how law has kept women subordinate and how to change it.
Liberal feminists seek real equality; difference feminists want law to recognise real differences; dominance theory (MacKinnon) sees law as male power.

manas.q: Name three strands of feminist legal theory.

children.note: Kimberlé Crenshaw showed that race, sex and class can combine to create disadvantages that single-issue law misses.
Should law enforce morality, and what makes a society just?
Arising from proposals to decriminalise homosexuality in the UK: Lord Devlin said law may enforce shared morality; Hart disagreed.

manas.q: What was the Hart–Devlin debate about?

children.note: John Rawls asked what rules people would choose for society if they did not know their own place in it.
In the "original position" you do not know your class, wealth or talents, so you cannot rig the rules for yourself.

manas.q: What is Rawls's veil of ignorance?

children.note: First, equal basic liberties for all (this comes first). Second, fair equality of opportunity, and inequalities only if they help the worst-off (difference principle).

manas.q: What is the difference principle?

children.note: Libertarian replies: Robert Nozick defended a minimal state; Friedrich Hayek stressed the rule of law and spontaneous order.

children.topic: Example: a land dispute in Kiambu
children.note: Two families claim the same plot. A positivist asks what the register says; a natural lawyer asks what is just; Rawls asks what rule you would accept not knowing which family you are.
African ideas about law and the place of customary law in Kenya today.
Long-standing community practices that become binding because people treat them as obligatory.

manas.q: What is customary law?

children.note: Studies of African customary systems show rules applied flexibly to the facts of each dispute, aiming to restore relationships.
"A person is a person through other persons." Justice focuses on repairing relationships through apology, restitution and reconciliation.
Any law, including customary law, that conflicts with the Constitution is invalid to that extent.

manas.q: What happens to customary law that conflicts with Kenya's Constitution?

children.note: Courts must promote reconciliation, mediation, arbitration and traditional dispute resolution, but not where it breaks the Bill of Rights, justice and morality, or written law.

manas.q: What limits does Article 159 put on traditional dispute resolution?

children.note: Wambui Otieno and her husband's Umira Kager clan fought over where to bury him. The Court of Appeal applied Luo custom and gave the clan the burial.

manas.q: What did the Court of Appeal decide in the S.M. Otieno burial dispute?

children.note: It shows the clash between custom and the individual, and between the historical school and positivist written law.
Add the leading Kenyan decisions from Kenya Law (kenyalaw.org).
Most exam questions are essays: "Discuss" a claim about law.
State the question's claim, explain two or three schools that answer it, compare them, then give your own reasoned view.
"An unjust law is not law. Discuss." Explain Aquinas and Fuller, then Hart's separation thesis, use the grudge informer, then apply to a Kenyan example.
Tie theory to the Constitution 2010: supremacy of the Constitution, customary law, and the courts' value-based interpretation.
Mistakes examiners often see.
Wrong. Positivists say a bad law is still law, but can be criticised and disobeyed on moral grounds.
Austin: commands and sanctions. Hart: rules, including power-giving rules, and the rule of recognition.
Marks come from comparing theories and judging them, not reciting who said what.
Videos to see the debates explained, then pages to read further.

Mahela Liyanage on whether morality is part of law.
Jeffrey Kaplan on Dworkin's critique of Hart's theory.
