maps.title: Equity and the Law of Trusts

nodeData.topic: Equity and the Law of Trusts
nodeData.note: Equity is the body of fairness rules that sits beside the common law, and the trust is its main creation. This map covers equity's history and maxims, its remedies, how trusts are made and enforced, and how Kenya receives these rules. A draft study aid, not legal advice.

children.topic: What equity is and why it matters
children.note: Equity is a set of fairness rules that grew up beside the ordinary common law. It steps in when strict rules would give an unfair result. Trusts are its biggest invention.
Early common law worked through fixed forms of action and money damages. If your case did not fit a form, you had no remedy. People then asked the King's Chancellor for a fair outcome.

manas.q: Why did equity develop beside the common law?

children.note: Petitions to the Chancellor grew into a separate court, the Court of Chancery. It judged the conscience of the defendant, not just the strict wording of the law.
In the Earl of Oxford's case, a quarrel between Chancery and the common-law judges was settled for the Crown: where equity and common law conflict, equity prevails.

manas.q: What rule came out of the Earl of Oxford's case (1615)?

children.note: These English Acts joined the two court systems so one court can apply both. They merged the courts, not the two bodies of rules, so equity is still a separate set of principles.

manas.q: Did the Judicature Acts fuse common law and equity?

children.note: Equity lets one person hold the legal title while another enjoys the benefit (the equitable or beneficial interest). This split is the heart of every trust.

manas.q: What is the difference between legal and equitable ownership?

children.note: Damages at common law come as of right once you prove a wrong. Equitable remedies are given at the court's choice, looking at all the facts and the parties' conduct.
Equity sums up its thinking in short sayings called maxims. They are guides, not strict rules, and help you argue whether relief should be given.
A person who has behaved badly in the very matter cannot ask equity for help. In D & C Builders v Rees, Lord Denning refused equitable relief to people who had pressured a struggling builder.

manas.q: What does 'he who comes to equity must come with clean hands' mean?

children.topic: Treats as done what ought to be done
children.note: If a person is bound to do something, equity acts as if it is already done. Walsh v Lonsdale used this to treat an agreement for a lease as a lease in equity.

manas.q: Which case illustrates 'equity looks on as done that which ought to be done'?

children.note: If you ask for a fair remedy, you must be ready to act fairly too, for example by repaying money you received.
A person who sleeps on their rights for too long, harming the other side, may lose an equitable remedy. This is called laches.
Equity does not throw away the common law. It works alongside it and steps in only where strict law would be unfair.
Equity's orders are aimed at the defendant personally (in personam). Disobeying an injunction is contempt of court.
When money is not enough, equity offers orders that make people do, stop, undo or correct things. All are discretionary.

children.topic: Injunction: an order to stop or act
children.note: An injunction orders a person to stop doing something (prohibitory) or to do something (mandatory). Example: stopping a neighbour from building on your access road.
In American Cyanamid v Ethicon (1975) the House of Lords asked: is there a serious question to be tried, are damages adequate, and where does the balance of convenience lie?

manas.q: What is the American Cyanamid test for an interim injunction?

children.note: An order to carry out a contract as promised. It is common for land, because each plot is treated as unique, so money cannot buy an exact substitute.

manas.q: Why is specific performance usually available for contracts to sell land?

children.note: Courts usually refuse it where damages are enough, for personal service contracts, where constant supervision would be needed, or where the claimant has unclean hands.
Rescission cancels a contract and puts the parties back where they started, for example after a misrepresentation. It is lost if that return is no longer possible.
If a written contract does not record what the parties truly agreed, the court can correct the wording to match the real agreement.
A wrongdoer is made to hand over the profit they made, rather than paying the claimant's loss. It is common against disloyal trustees and fiduciaries.
An express trust is one a person sets up on purpose. To work it needs clear words, proper form and property actually moved into it.
A trust is an arrangement where one person (the trustee) holds property for the benefit of others (the beneficiaries). The person who sets it up is the settlor.

manas.q: Who are the three parties to a trust?

children.note: Knight v Knight (1840) set the test: a trust needs certainty of intention, of subject matter and of objects (beneficiaries). If one fails, there is no trust.

manas.q: What are the three certainties, and which case set them out?

children.note: The settlor must really mean to create a trust, not just hope or wish. No special words are needed: in Paul v Constance a couple's casual words about a bank account were enough.

manas.q: Do you need the word 'trust' to create a trust?

children.note: You must be able to say exactly which property is held on trust and what share each beneficiary gets. 'Most of my money' is too vague.
You must be able to identify who the beneficiaries are. Otherwise the court cannot supervise the trustees.
Some trusts need writing. A trust in a will must follow the will rules of the Law of Succession Act. For land, written evidence is wise; reviewer to confirm the exact Kenyan rule.
A trust only binds once the property is properly in the trustee's hands. Milroy v Lord gave three routes: give it outright, transfer it to trustees, or declare yourself trustee.

children.topic: Equity will not perfect a gift
children.note: If a gift fails for want of the right steps, equity will not rescue it by calling it a trust. A volunteer (someone who gave nothing) cannot force completion.

manas.q: Will equity save a failed gift by treating it as a trust?

children.topic: Re Rose: done all he could
children.note: In Re Rose, a share gift took effect in equity once the donor had completed everything in his own power, even though registration came later.
In Saunders v Vautier (1841), adult beneficiaries of sound mind who together own the whole benefit can end the trust and take the property.

manas.q: What does the rule in Saunders v Vautier allow beneficiaries to do?

children.note: In a fixed trust each beneficiary's share is set. In a discretionary trust the trustees choose who gets what, within a group the settlor named.
A charitable trust is for a purpose, not named people. It must be charitable and benefit the public or a section of it.
The classic categories are relief of poverty, advancement of education, advancement of religion and other purposes beneficial to the community.

manas.q: What are the four classic heads of charity?

children.note: A charity must help the public or a real section of it, not a private circle such as one family or one firm's staff.
If a charitable purpose becomes impossible, the court can redirect the gift to a similar charitable purpose instead of letting it fail.
In Kenya, trustees of a charitable trust often register as one body under the Trustees (Perpetual Succession) Act so the trust can hold land and sue.
Some trusts arise without anyone declaring them. The law implies them from the facts to stop unfair results.
Here the benefit 'jumps back' to the person who provided the property, for example when a trust fails or someone pays for property put in another's name.

manas.q: What is a resulting trust?

children.topic: Paying for land in another's name
children.note: If Wanjiru pays for a plot but registers it in her brother's name, equity may presume he holds it for her unless he shows it was a gift.

children.topic: Money lent for a stated purpose
children.note: In Barclays Bank v Quistclose, money lent only to pay a dividend was held on trust when that purpose failed, so the lender got it back ahead of other creditors.
A constructive trust is imposed by law where it would be against conscience for the holder to keep property for himself, for example profits from a breach of loyalty.

manas.q: When does a constructive trust arise?

children.note: Where a home is in one partner's name, the other may still have a share through a common intention constructive trust. English cases include Lloyds Bank v Rosset and Stack v Dowden.
Kenyan courts also recognise trusts arising from customary land holding, such as land registered in one family member's name for the clan. Reviewer to add the leading Kenyan cases.
Trustees must be loyal and careful. If they break the trust, they pay, and the beneficiaries can follow the property.
A trustee must not let personal interest clash with duty, and must not make an unauthorised profit from the role.

manas.q: What is the trustee's core duty of loyalty?

children.note: A trustee must act like an ordinary prudent business person managing their own affairs, as Speight v Gaunt (1883) held.

manas.q: What standard of care did Speight v Gaunt set for trustees?

children.note: Trustees must be even-handed, for example not favouring someone with life income over those who get the capital later.
Trustees must keep records, account for the property and give beneficiaries proper information about the trust.
Trustees have powers from the trust deed and the Trustee Act, such as investing, appointing agents, and using funds for a beneficiary's upkeep or education.
Any failure to follow the trust or the duties is a breach. The trustee must restore the loss to the trust fund.
A stranger who dishonestly helps a breach is personally liable. Royal Brunei Airlines v Tan (1995) said the test is whether he acted as an honest person would.

manas.q: What is the test for dishonest assistance in Royal Brunei Airlines v Tan?

links.label: Royal Brunei Airlines v Tan, Wikipedia

children.note: Tracing lets beneficiaries identify trust property, or what it was swapped for, in someone else's hands and claim it back.

manas.q: What is tracing?

children.note: If a trustee mixes trust money with his own and spends some, Re Hallett (1880) presumes he spent his own money first, leaving the trust money in the account.

manas.q: What did Re Hallett's Estate presume about a mixed account?

children.note: Re Diplock held that people wrongly paid from an estate could be made to repay, and allowed tracing into mixed funds held by innocent charities.
A trustee may escape liability where the beneficiary agreed to the act, where the claim is too late, or where the court relieves an honest and reasonable trustee.
Kenya received English equity and trust law, and has its own statutes on top. Kenyan rules can differ, so always check the Kenyan Act.
The Judicature Act lets Kenyan courts apply the common law, doctrines of equity and old English statutes of general application, as at a fixed date, where Kenyan law is silent.

manas.q: Which Kenyan Act brings English equity into Kenyan law?

children.note: Received English rules apply only so far as they fit the Constitution and Kenyan written law, and Kenyan circumstances.
Article 159 tells courts to do justice without undue regard to procedural technicalities and to promote alternative and traditional dispute resolution. This echoes equity's fairness.

manas.q: Which Article of the Constitution tells courts not to be ruled by technicalities?

children.note: Kenya's Trustee Act sets trustees' powers of investment, appointment and retirement, and lets the court relieve honest trustees. It follows the older English model.
This Act lets trustees of a charitable or community body register as one incorporated body that continues even when individual trustees change.
Trusts often arise when a person dies. This Act governs wills and estates, and administrators hold the estate on a kind of trust for heirs.
Add the leading Kenyan decisions from Kenya Law (kenyalaw.org).
These classic English cases are cited in Kenyan courts too. Learn the name, the facts in one line and the rule.
A trustee renewed a lease for himself after the landlord refused to renew it for the child beneficiary. He had to hand it over: no conflict of interest allowed.

manas.q: What rule does Keech v Sandford stand for?

children.note: A solicitor who used information from the trust to make a profit held it on constructive trust, though he acted honestly. He got an allowance for his work.

manas.q: Why did Boardman have to give up his profit in Boardman v Phipps?

children.note: The House of Lords held a bank paid under a void swap deal had no resulting trust, stressing that the recipient's conscience must be affected.
A mail-order firm put customers' money in a separate account. That money was held on trust, so the customers were safe when the firm went insolvent.
An agreement for a lease was treated as a lease in equity, because equity treats as done what ought to be done.
A singer could not be forced to sing, but an injunction stopped her singing for a rival. Equity can enforce a negative promise.
Use IRAC: Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion. Work through each certainty or duty one at a time.
Before he died, Mzee Kamau wrote 'I hope my son Njoroge will look after the family with some of my land.' Is there a trust for the family?
Did Mzee Kamau create a valid express trust of the land for the family?
Knight v Knight: a trust needs certainty of intention, subject matter and objects. Words of hope may show only a wish.
'I hope' suggests a wish, not a binding duty. 'Some of my land' is unclear property, and 'the family' may be unclear objects. Consider a customary trust argument too.
Likely no express trust, so Njoroge may take the land free of it, unless a customary trust or a resulting trust can be shown. Note both sides.

children.topic: Trap: wish is not a trust
children.note: Precatory words such as 'hope', 'wish' or 'trust and confidence' usually do not create a trust. Read the words carefully.

children.topic: Trap: failed gift as a trust
children.note: Do not argue that a failed gift becomes a trust. Milroy v Lord rejects this.
Equitable remedies are not automatic. Always discuss clean hands, delay and whether damages are enough.
Always add the Kenyan angle: Judicature Act reception, the Trustee Act and customary trusts.

The Law Academy runs through the main maxims of equity with simple examples.
The Law Academy explains intention, subject matter and objects for a valid trust.
The Law Academy explains when and why a resulting trust arises.
The Law Academy explains constructive trusts and how courts impose them.
Digestible Law walks through how tracing works in equity, including mixed funds.
History of Chancery, the maxims and the equitable remedies.
Parties, types of trust and trustees' duties.
The Council of Legal Education list of core LLB courses, including Equity and the Law of Trusts.

nodeData.note: Property law decides who owns land and what rights others can hold over it. This map covers the Constitution's land chapter, tenure, the 2012 and 2016 land Acts, registration, leases, easements, charges, adverse possession, co-ownership and land disputes. A draft study aid, not legal advice.

children.note: Property law is about who may own, use and control things, and what rights others can hold over them. Land is the most important and most fought-over kind of property in Kenya.

children.topic: Rights over things, not just things
children.note: Owning property means holding a bundle of rights: to use it, keep others out, sell it, lease it or leave it to heirs.

manas.q: Why is property described as a 'bundle of rights'?

children.topic: Land includes what is fixed to it
children.note: In law, land is the ground plus buildings and things firmly attached (fixtures), such as a house or a fence. A parked car is not part of the land.

manas.q: What are fixtures?

children.note: A property right binds the whole world (in rem), while a contract right binds only the other party (in personam). That is why buyers of land must check for others' rights.

manas.q: What is the difference between a right in rem and a right in personam?

children.note: Some rights are legal; others exist only in equity, such as a beneficiary's share under a trust. Your Equity and Trusts course explains the split.
Land is home, farm, savings and family identity. Disputes over a plot in Kiambu or a ranch in Laikipia can last for decades, which is why the Constitution gives land its own chapter.
Chapter Five (Land and Environment) sets the big rules. Article 40 in the Bill of Rights protects property itself.

Everyone may acquire and own property anywhere in Kenya. The State may take it only for a public purpose, by law, with prompt full and just compensation. Unlawfully acquired property is not protected.

manas.q: On what terms may the State compulsorily acquire property under Article 40?

children.note: Land must be held and used fairly, efficiently, productively and sustainably. Principles include equal access, security of rights, clear and cheap administration, and no gender discrimination.

manas.q: Name three principles of land policy in Article 60.

children.note: All land belongs to the people of Kenya collectively as a nation, as communities and as individuals. It is classified as public, community or private.

manas.q: What are the three classes of land under Article 61?

children.note: Includes unalienated government land, land used by State organs, forests, game reserves, national parks, rivers, lakes, minerals and the sea bed. It is held by county or national government and managed by the NLC.

manas.q: Give four examples of public land under Article 62.

children.note: Land held by communities sharing ethnicity, culture or similar interest, such as grazing areas, shrines, ancestral lands and community forests. Unregistered community land is held in trust by county governments.

manas.q: Who holds unregistered community land under Article 63?

children.note: Private land is registered land held under freehold, land held under leasehold, and any other land Parliament declares private.
Non-citizens may hold land only on leasehold, for at most 99 years. A longer grant is cut down to 99 years. A company counts as a citizen only if wholly owned by citizens.

manas.q: What is the maximum lease a non-citizen may hold under Article 65?

children.note: The NLC manages public land for both levels of government, recommends land policy, investigates historical land injustices and encourages traditional dispute resolution.

manas.q: Name three functions of the National Land Commission under Article 67.

children.note: Parliament must revise land laws, set minimum and maximum holdings, protect matrimonial property (especially the matrimonial home) and protect dependants of deceased landholders.
Tenure means the terms on which you hold land. The 2012 and 2016 Acts put Chapter Five into practice.
Freehold gives ownership with no end date. You may use, sell, charge or leave the land to heirs, subject to planning and other laws.

manas.q: What is freehold tenure?

children.note: Leasehold gives exclusive use for a fixed term, usually in return for rent. When it ends, the land goes back to the landlord, often the government or county.

manas.q: What is leasehold tenure?

children.note: Many rural families hold land by custom or as part of a community. The Community Land Act 2016 now lets communities register and manage such land.
Covers management of public land, compulsory acquisition, leases, charges (mortgages) and easements. The NLC has many duties under it.
The main law on registering land and interests, opening land registers and issuing titles. It replaced several older registration laws.

manas.q: Which Act governs registration of land titles in Kenya today?

children.note: Sets out how the NLC is run and adds to its constitutional functions, such as keeping a land information system.
Gives effect to Article 63. A community registers, forms a community assembly and can hold title to its land as one group.
Many dealings in agricultural land need consent from a local Land Control Board. Without consent, the deal may be void.
Lets flats or units in one building be owned separately, with shared parts like stairs held in common.
Kenya uses title registration: the register, not a pile of old deeds, shows who owns what.
Registration makes ownership easy to check and hard to fake. A buyer searches the register instead of tracing decades of documents.
The register should mirror the true position; buyers need not look behind it (curtain); people who lose through registry error may be compensated (indemnity).

manas.q: What are the mirror, curtain and indemnity principles?

children.topic: Title deed and certificate of lease
children.note: Freehold land gets a title deed; leasehold land gets a certificate of lease. The register entry is what counts.
Before buying, search the register at the land registry to confirm the owner and any charges, cautions or restrictions.
A registered title is strongly protected, but the Land Registration Act lets courts cancel a title gained by fraud, misrepresentation or a corrupt or illegal process.

manas.q: When can a registered title in Kenya be challenged?

children.note: Some rights bind a buyer even though they are not on the register, such as certain short leases, rights of people in occupation and, in Kenya, spousal and customary trust rights. Check the Act's list.

manas.q: What are overriding interests?

children.note: A person claiming an interest can lodge a caution to warn buyers and stop dealings until the claim is dealt with.
Besides ownership, people can hold lesser rights over someone else's land.
A lease gives exclusive possession for a fixed or periodic term, usually for rent. A mere permission to use land is only a licence.

manas.q: What is the key feature that separates a lease from a licence?

children.topic: Easements: rights over a neighbour's land
children.note: An easement is a right one plot enjoys over another, such as a footpath to the road or a pipe across the next shamba.
Re Ellenborough Park: there must be a benefiting and a burdened plot, the right must help the benefiting land, the owners must differ, and the right must be grantable.

manas.q: What are the four Re Ellenborough Park tests for an easement?

children.note: Power lines and pipelines cross private land under wayleaves. The NLC approves wayleaves under the Land Act.
A charge gives a lender security over land for a loan. If the borrower defaults, the lender may, after giving proper notice, sell the land to recover the debt.
The borrower who gives the security is the chargor; the lender is the chargee.

manas.q: In a charge, who is the chargor and who is the chargee?

children.note: After default and statutory notice, the chargee may sue, appoint a receiver, take possession or sell. Sale must be fair and get a proper price.
The borrower can always clear the debt and get the land back free of the charge. Clauses that block redemption are unfair.
Where the land is a matrimonial home, the lender should check spousal consent. Reviewer to confirm the exact rule in the Land Act.
A person who occupies another's land openly, without permission and without a break for the full limitation period may become owner. Kenya's period is in the Limitation of Actions Act.
Actual, open, exclusive and continuous possession, against the owner's rights and without permission, for the whole period.

manas.q: What must a squatter prove to claim adverse possession?

children.note: A tenant or a relative allowed to stay is not adverse. In BP Properties v Buckler, a permission to stay defeated the claim.
Two or more people can own the same land together.
Joint tenants own the whole together. When one dies, the others take the whole automatically, outside the will.

manas.q: What happens on a joint tenant's death?

children.note: Tenants in common hold separate shares, such as half each. A share passes under the owner's will or estate.

manas.q: How does a tenancy in common differ from a joint tenancy?

children.note: Article 68 requires protection of matrimonial property, especially the matrimonial home. The Matrimonial Property Act 2013 sets the rules on rights during and after marriage.
Land cases go to a special court, but the Constitution also encourages local and traditional solutions.
Article 162 requires Parliament to set up a court with High Court status for disputes over the environment and the use, occupation of and title to land.

manas.q: Which Article creates a court with High Court status for land disputes?

children.note: This Act sets up the court and its powers. Lower-value land cases may be heard by magistrates' courts.
Article 159 promotes mediation, arbitration and traditional dispute resolution, and Article 60 encourages local community land solutions.
The NLC can investigate past land injustices and recommend redress. In 2015 the Supreme Court said the NLC oversees processes leading to registration but does not register titles itself.
Add the leading Kenyan decisions from Kenya Law (kenyalaw.org).
Classic English cases Kenyan courts cite as persuasive. Kenyan statute always comes first.
A deal called a 'licence' was really a lease, because it gave exclusive possession for a term at a rent. Labels do not decide.

manas.q: What did Street v Mountford decide about leases and licences?

children.note: The Court of Appeal set the four characteristics of an easement, using a shared private garden.
A wife not on the title but living in the house had a share, and her actual occupation bound the bank.

manas.q: Why did the bank lose in Williams & Glyn's Bank v Boland?

children.note: Farmers who used land for years kept their adverse possession claim. The European human rights court later accepted such rules.
A couple held a jointly registered home in unequal shares, with the woman getting 65%, inferred from all the circumstances.
An agreement for a lease was treated as a lease in equity, since equity treats as done what ought to be done.
Use IRAC. Start with the class of land and the register, then look for unregistered rights.
Otieno buys a registered plot in Kiambu. He then finds Mama Njeri has farmed one corner openly for many years without anyone's permission. Can she stop him?
Does Mama Njeri have a right that binds Otieno though it is not on the register?
Adverse possession needs open, exclusive, uninterrupted possession without consent for the full period in the Limitation of Actions Act. Such rights can bind a buyer.
Check her years on the land, whether any owner ever gave permission, and whether she has applied to court. Otieno's search would not show her claim.
If she proves all elements for the full period, she may get title to that corner. Otieno's remedy may lie against the seller.

children.topic: Trap: title deed is not everything
children.note: Overriding interests, fraud and adverse possession can defeat a buyer who only checked the title.
Older registration laws were replaced in 2012. Use the Land Act and Land Registration Act.
Non-citizens cannot hold freehold. Article 65 limits them to leases of up to 99 years.
In any sale or charge of a family home, discuss the spouse's rights under the Matrimonial Property Act and Article 68.

nodeData.note: Treaties, custom, states, the UN, human rights and international courts.

children.note: The rules that bind countries and international bodies: where they come from, how treaties work, when force is allowed, and how it all reaches Kenya. A study aid for LLB students, not legal advice.

nodeData.note: The rules that bind countries and international bodies: where they come from, how treaties work, when force is allowed, and how it all reaches Kenya. A study aid for LLB students, not legal advice.

children.note: Start here: who the law is for, why states obey it, and how it reaches ordinary people.
International law is the set of rules that countries (states) accept as binding in their dealings with each other. Think of it as the rulebook of the international community.

manas.q: What is public international law?

children.note: Public international law governs states and international bodies. Private international law (conflict of laws) decides which country's law applies to a private dispute, such as a cross-border sale.
There is no world parliament, police or compulsory court. Rules are made mostly by states agreeing, and they are kept through consent, reciprocity and reputation.
States are the main subjects. International organisations such as the UN are also subjects, and individuals now have rights (human rights) and duties (international crimes).

manas.q: Who are the subjects of international law?

children.topic: Why it matters to a Kenyan
children.note: Trade deals, the EAC common market, refugee protection and human rights complaints all rest on international law. It shapes daily life more than it seems.
Monist systems treat international law as part of national law automatically. Dualist systems need a national law to bring it in. Kenya's 2010 Constitution moved Kenya towards monism.

manas.q: What is the difference between monism and dualism?

children.note: Where do the rules come from? The usual list is in Article 38(1) of the Statute of the International Court of Justice.
Treaties, custom, general principles of law, and (as helpers) court decisions and the writings of experts. Article 38 sets no ranking among them.

manas.q: What four sources does Article 38(1) of the ICJ Statute list?

children.note: Written agreements that states sign and accept. They bind only the states that agree to them, like a contract between countries.
Custom needs two things: states actually behave a certain way (state practice), and they do so because they believe the law requires it (opinio juris).

manas.q: What two elements make up customary international law?

children.note: The practice should be common and consistent, with wide participation, especially by the states most affected. It need not be universal.
A state that objects clearly and consistently while a custom is forming may avoid being bound by it. Holding out alone is hard in practice.
Ideas shared by the world's legal systems, such as good faith or that a wrong must be repaired. They fill gaps when no treaty or custom applies.
These are subsidiary means: they help find and explain the rules but are not sources on their own. ICJ judgments bind only the parties to the case (Article 59).
A small group of rules no state may contract out of, such as the bans on genocide, slavery, torture and aggressive war. A treaty that clashes with them is void.

manas.q: What is jus cogens?

children.note: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties is the 'law of contracts' for countries.
Adopted in 1969 and in force from 1980. Much of it is accepted as reflecting customary law, so it guides even states that never joined.

manas.q: When was the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties adopted and when did it come into force?

children.note: A written agreement between states, governed by international law, whatever it is called: treaty, convention, protocol or charter.
Pacta sunt servanda: a treaty in force binds its parties, who must perform it in good faith (VCLT Article 26).

manas.q: What does pacta sunt servanda mean?

children.note: When joining a treaty, a state may sometimes declare that it will not be bound by a particular clause (Article 19), unless the treaty forbids it.
Articles 31 to 33: read the words in good faith, in context, and in light of the treaty's purpose. Drafting history is a supplementary aid only.

children.topic: Void if it breaks jus cogens
children.note: Article 53: a treaty that conflicts with a peremptory rule (jus cogens) is void.
Article 62 allows a party to rely on a fundamental, unforeseen change of circumstances only in narrow cases (rebus sic stantibus).
Signing usually shows intent; ratifying is the formal step that makes a state bound. Many students mix these two up.
Who counts as a state, when it may apply its laws, and when it is shielded from other countries' courts.
Montevideo Convention 1933, Article 1: a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to deal with other states.

manas.q: What are the four Montevideo criteria for statehood?

children.note: Declaratory theory: recognition only confirms a state that already exists. Constitutive theory: recognition creates the state's legal personality.

manas.q: What is the difference between the declaratory and constitutive theories of recognition?

children.note: Prescriptive jurisdiction is a state's power to make laws. Adjudicative jurisdiction is its courts' power to hear cases.
Territory, nationality of the offender, nationality of the victim (passive personality), protection of the state's security, and universal jurisdiction.

manas.q: Name the five bases of criminal jurisdiction.

children.note: For the gravest crimes, such as piracy, any state may prosecute, whoever did it and wherever it happened.
States were once fully immune from other countries' courts. The modern restrictive view covers governmental acts but not ordinary commercial deals.

manas.q: What is the restrictive theory of state immunity?

children.note: Acta jure imperii (acts of state power, such as defence) attract immunity; acta jure gestionis (commercial acts, such as buying cement) usually do not.
What happens when a state breaks the rules, and when (if ever) it may use force.
The International Law Commission's 2001 Articles on State Responsibility set out the general rules; the UN General Assembly commended them to states.

children.topic: Two elements of a wrongful act
children.note: An internationally wrongful act needs (1) conduct that can be attributed to the state and (2) a breach of an international obligation.

manas.q: What two elements make an internationally wrongful act?

children.note: Officials and state organs count, even when they exceed their powers. So do groups acting under the state's direction or control.
Consent, self-defence, countermeasures, force majeure, distress and necessity can excuse what would otherwise be a breach.
The state must stop the wrong and make full reparation: restitution (restore), compensation (pay), or satisfaction (for example an apology).

manas.q: What three forms can reparation take?

children.note: Article 2 of the UN Charter (1945) requires members to refrain from the threat or use of force against other states. It is close to absolute.
Under Chapter VII the Security Council decides if peace is threatened (Article 39) and may authorise military action (Article 42).
Article 51 keeps the right of individual or collective self-defence if an armed attack occurs, until the Security Council acts. It must be reported to the Council.

manas.q: Which UN Charter article preserves the right of self-defence, and what triggers it?

children.note: Rights for people, and the courts that hear disputes and prosecute crimes.
The African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights was adopted in Nairobi in 1981 and came into force in 1986.

manas.q: Where and when was the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights adopted?

children.note: Unusually, the Charter protects group rights (self-determination, natural resources, development, a satisfactory environment) and lists duties individuals owe.
The Commission, now based in Banjul, The Gambia, monitors and interprets the Charter and hears complaints.
A 1998 protocol set up the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights; it came into force in 2004.
The UN's main court, at the Peace Palace in The Hague, set up in 1945. Fifteen judges serve nine-year terms; it hears disputes between states only.

manas.q: How many judges sit on the ICJ, and who can be parties in its contentious cases?

children.note: A state is bound only if it agreed: by special agreement, a treaty clause, or an optional-clause declaration under Article 36(2). It also gives advisory opinions.
The International Criminal Court (Rome Statute 1998, working since 2002) tries people for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and aggression.

manas.q: Which four crimes can the ICC try?

children.note: Complementarity: the ICC acts only when national courts are unwilling or unable to prosecute genuinely.
The ICC prosecutor opened a formal investigation into Kenya in 2010 after the 2007–08 violence. Uhuru Kenyatta and William Ruto were among those charged; no one was convicted.
How international law enters Kenyan law, and Kenya's regional community.
The general rules of international law form part of Kenyan law automatically.

manas.q: What does Article 2(5) of the Constitution of Kenya say about international law?

children.note: Any treaty or convention Kenya has ratified becomes part of Kenyan law under the Constitution.

manas.q: Under Article 2(6), when does a treaty become part of Kenyan law?

children.note: Under the old constitution, a treaty generally needed an Act of Parliament before Kenyan courts would apply it. The 2010 text changed this.
The Treaty Making and Ratification Act 2012 sets the steps Kenya follows to negotiate and ratify treaties, including a role for Parliament.
Treaty signed 1999, in force 2000, headquarters in Arusha. Members: Burundi, DR Congo, Kenya, Rwanda, Somalia, South Sudan, Tanzania and Uganda.
Customs union (2005), common market (2010), a planned monetary union, and in the long run political federation.
Based in Arusha, it interprets the EAC Treaty. Individuals and states can bring cases; on Treaty matters it prevails over national courts.
Maritime Delimitation in the Indian Ocean: the ICJ gave judgment on the sea boundary in October 2021. Kenya said it does not recognise the judgment.
Add the leading Kenyan decisions from Kenya Law (kenyalaw.org).
Classic decisions every student meets. Learn the one-line point of each.
A French ship hit a Turkish ship on the high seas. Turkey tried the French officer. The court held no rule stopped Turkey, so states are free unless a rule forbids them.

manas.q: What principle comes from the Lotus case?

children.note: The ICJ explained that custom needs practice plus a belief it is legally required (opinio juris), and that a treaty rule can grow into custom.
The ICJ refused to find a regional custom where state practice was too inconsistent.
The US broke customary law by mining Nicaragua's ports and backing rebels. Its collective self-defence claim failed because there was no armed attack.

manas.q: Why did the USA's self-defence argument fail in Nicaragua v USA?

children.note: An ICJ advisory opinion recognising that the UN itself is a subject of international law with its own legal personality.
The ICJ said using nuclear weapons would generally clash with humanitarian law, but could not decide the case of extreme self-defence.
Use IRAC, then watch for the classic traps.
Name the legal question in one line: for example, did State A lawfully use force, or is this rule binding on State B?
State the rule and its source: treaty article, custom (practice plus opinio juris), or a leading ICJ case.
Apply each element of the rule to the facts, one by one. Say which facts help each side.
Give a clear, reasoned answer. If the facts are unclear, say what extra fact would change the result.
A foreign trawler is seized off Lamu and its captain is tried in Mombasa. Issue: jurisdiction. Rule: territorial and protective bases. Apply: where was the boat? Conclude.
A state that only signed a treaty is not yet bound by it as a party. Check the ratification step.
Practice alone is not enough. Always prove opinio juris as well.
Do not assume the ICJ can hear any dispute. Check how each state accepted its jurisdiction.

children.topic: Trap: Kenya is not purely dualist
children.note: After 2010, Articles 2(5) and 2(6) bring international law into Kenyan law. Older textbooks may say otherwise.

children.note: The law of work in Kenya: who is an employee, minimum terms under the Employment Act 2007, fair dismissal, unions and strikes, safety, and the ELRC. A study aid, not legal advice.

nodeData.note: The law of work in Kenya: who is an employee, minimum terms under the Employment Act 2007, fair dismissal, unions and strikes, safety, and the ELRC. A study aid, not legal advice.

children.note: The rules for work: between one worker and an employer, and between unions and employers as groups.
Labour (employment) law sets the rights and duties of employers and workers: pay, hours, safety, leave, discipline and dismissal.

manas.q: What does labour law cover?

children.note: Individual labour law is about one worker's contract. Collective labour law is about trade unions, bargaining and strikes.
A worker usually has less bargaining power than an employer. The law sets minimum terms that a contract cannot go below.
Employment is a contract, so Year 1 Contract ideas apply. Workplace injuries also link to negligence in Torts.
A casual worker on a Nairobi building site paid daily still has legal protection. Which protection depends on how long and how regularly they work.
The first question in most problems: is this person an employee at all? Only employees get most statutory protection.

children.topic: Contract of service vs for services
children.note: An employee works under a contract of service. An independent contractor (like a fundi hired for one job) works under a contract for services.

manas.q: What is the difference between a contract of service and a contract for services?

children.note: A driver who bought his own lorry, paid its costs and was paid per load was held to be a contractor, not an employee, despite wearing the company's colours.
1) The worker gives personal work and skill for pay; 2) the employer has enough control; 3) the other terms fit an employment contract.

manas.q: What three conditions did Ready Mixed Concrete set for a contract of employment?

children.note: Calling someone a 'contractor' in the paperwork does not settle it. Courts look at the real relationship.
Who controls how and when work is done? Who owns the tools? Who bears the risk of loss? Can the worker send a substitute?
Employees get leave, notice, unfair dismissal protection and work injury cover. Contractors mostly rely on their contract alone.
The Employment Act 2007 sets the minimum terms of every employment in Kenya.
The Act sets a floor. A clause giving a worker less than the Act provides does not take away the worker's statutory rights.

manas.q: Can an employer and worker agree to terms below the Employment Act's minimum?

children.note: A contract expected to last three months or more must be put in writing, and the employer must keep employment records.
A casual worker who keeps working continuously for a long period can be treated as on a monthly contract, with fuller protection.
Wages must be paid in money and on time. Unlawful deductions are not allowed. Minimum wages are set by government wage orders.
After twelve months of service, a worker is entitled to at least 21 working days of paid annual leave.

manas.q: How much paid annual leave must a Kenyan employee get after 12 months' service?

children.note: A female employee gets three months' maternity leave on full pay. A male employee gets two weeks' paternity leave.

manas.q: How long are maternity and paternity leave under the Employment Act?

children.note: Paid sick leave is available after two months' service, with medical proof. Rest days and limits on hours are also protected.

A termination is lawful only if the employer has a valid reason (conduct, capacity or operational needs) AND follows a fair procedure.

manas.q: What two things must an employer show for a termination to be fair?

children.note: Before dismissal for misconduct or poor performance, the worker must be told the reasons and heard, with a colleague or union official present.
In an unfair termination claim, the burden is on the employer to prove the reason was valid and fair.

manas.q: Who bears the burden of proving the reason for termination?

children.note: Dismissal without notice is allowed only for gross misconduct, such as theft, being drunk on duty or serious insubordination. A hearing is still needed.
The worker resigns because the employer committed a serious breach of the contract. Western Excavating v Sharp: use the contract test, not just 'unreasonable'.

manas.q: What is constructive dismissal?

children.note: Losing a job because the post is no longer needed. The employer must notify the union and labour officer, select fairly, and pay severance.

manas.q: What must an employer do in a redundancy?

children.note: In a redundancy, the worker gets severance of at least 15 days' pay for each completed year of service.
The court may order reinstatement, re-engagement, or compensation of up to twelve months' gross pay, plus unpaid dues.

A written deal on pay and terms negotiated between a union and employer. Once registered it binds both sides.

manas.q: What is a collective bargaining agreement?

children.note: A trade dispute is first reported for conciliation. Only if that fails can parties strike, lock out or go to court.

Keeping workers safe, and compensating them when they are hurt.
Requires employers to provide a safe workplace, safe machinery, training and protective gear, and allows workplace inspections.
Workers must take care for their own safety and others', and use the protective equipment provided.
Gives compensation to employees injured or made ill by their work, without needing to prove the employer was negligent.

manas.q: What is the main idea of the Work Injury Benefits Act?

children.note: An injury must be reported to the employer and the Director of Occupational Safety and Health Services, who assesses compensation.

Labour rights are constitutional rights in Kenya, with their own specialised court.
Every person has the right to fair labour practices.

manas.q: What right does Article 41(1) give every person?

children.note: Workers have rights to fair pay, reasonable working conditions, to form and join a trade union, and to go on strike.

manas.q: List the four workers' rights in Article 41(2).

children.note: Employers may form and join employers' organisations. Unions and employers' bodies run their own affairs, and all may bargain collectively.
The Constitution told Parliament to set up a court with the status of the High Court for employment and labour disputes.

manas.q: Which court hears employment disputes in Kenya, and what is its status?

children.note: Set up by its own Act, it hears all employment and labour relations disputes. Appeals go to the Court of Appeal. Ordinary High Court is not the forum.

children.note: Governments, employers and workers all have a voice at the ILO. Kenya's own labour bodies follow the same three-way model.
